title: How to read money books critically
publisher: Artha Kavach original summary of a book's ideas (paraphrase, not a quotation; the author's opinion, not settled fact) — pending manual verification
text: Money books are useful but not neutral. Watch for survivorship bias (they feature people who succeeded, not those who tried the same thing and failed), advice tuned to one country's taxes and products (many are American), data from specific market eras, and incentives: some authors sell seminars, funds or services. Ask: does the claim have evidence beyond a story, does it fit your goals and risk, are the numbers valid for India, and what is the downside if it is wrong? Prefer ideas that are cheap to try and easy to reverse, such as automating savings, and be careful with ideas that involve leverage or concentration. Verify rules and rates on official sites, and consider a SEBI-registered adviser for personal decisions.
